tasks.title: List and inspect networks
tasks.instructions:
List the networks on your LXD server to see what's configured:

```bash
lxc network list
```

You should see at least `lxdbr0` — the default bridge created during `lxd init`. Now inspect its configuration to understand how it's set up:

```bash
lxc network show lxdbr0
```

The output shows the IPv4/IPv6 address range, whether NAT is enabled, and the DHCP settings. This is the network your instances connect to by default — understanding it helps when troubleshooting connectivity issues.

tasks.title: Create a new bridge network
tasks.instructions:
Create a second bridge network with a different subnet. Separate networks are useful for isolating environments — for example, putting test instances on a different network from production ones:

```bash
lxc network create test-bridge \
  --type=bridge \
  ipv4.address=10.20.20.1/24 \
  ipv4.nat=true
```

Verify it was created:
```bash
lxc network list
```

You should see both `lxdbr0` and `test-bridge`. The new bridge has its own subnet (10.20.20.x) with NAT enabled, so instances on it can reach the internet.

tasks.title: Launch an instance on the new network
tasks.instructions:
Launch a container connected to the new `test-bridge` network instead of the default. This demonstrates how to place instances on specific networks:

```bash
lxc launch ubuntu:24.04 net-test
```

Then move its network interface to the new bridge:
```bash
lxc config device set net-test eth0 network=test-bridge
```

Restart the instance so the new network takes effect:
```bash
lxc restart net-test
```

Verify the instance got an IP on the new subnet:
```bash
lxc list net-test
```

The IPV4 column should show an address in the 10.20.20.x range.
hints: The instance needs to be restarted for the network change to take effect.
lxc list net-test shows the IP assigned to the instance — it should be on 10.20.20.x.
